title: The Apology of David
author: P. Kyle McCarter Jr.
publisher: Journal of Biblical Literature 99/4 (1980): 489-504; reprinted in Reconsidering Israel and Judah: Recent Studies on the Deuteronomistic History, ed. Gary N. Knoppers and J. Gordon McConville (Eisenbrauns/Penn State University Press, 2000)
allowedUseNotes: Modern copyrighted journal article. Project stores only its own summary/paraphrase of the article's thesis, drawn from secondary description, not the article's own text; no reproduction of its argument's wording.
summary: McCarter's originating statement of the 'apology of David' reading, later foundational to his own 1984 Anchor Bible commentaries on 1-2 Samuel (mccarter-1984-ii-samuel). The thesis, as consistently described across independent secondary sources discussing the article: much of the David narrative in 1-2 Samuel is best read as a work of royal apologetic, shaped to answer real contemporary accusations that David had murdered or benefited from the convenient deaths of political rivals and predecessors on his path to the throne (Saul, Jonathan, Abner, Ish-bosheth, and later Amasa) rather than as neutral historical reportage. This project cites the article specifically for that framework as applied to 2 Samuel 3:36-37 (claim-public-response) — the narrative's explicit insistence that 'it had not been the king's will to put Abner to death,' read on this account as apologetic material defending David against a real, contemporary charge of complicity rather than a plain incidental report of public opinion.
